hints: Look closely at what is swapped on the carbon atom, Cl out and OH in, and think about what type of reaction that describes.
Notice the lone pairs on HO- attacking the positive carbon centre, that tells you what role the hydroxide ion is playing.
Check how the C-Cl bond breaks, with both electrons going to Cl-, and recall what that uneven splitting is called.
walkthrough:
**Spot the overall change**

Look at the starting material and the organic product. A Cl atom on the cyclopentane ring has been replaced by an OH group.

Overall: $\text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{OH} + \text{Cl}^-$

**Identify substitution and the nucleophile**

Replacing one atom or group by another is substitution, so statement 1 is correct. The $\text{OH}^-$ ion uses its lone pair to attack the electron-deficient carbon, donating electrons, so it is acting as a nucleophile. That makes statement 2 correct.

**Check the bond fission**

The curly arrow shows the C-Cl bond breaking with both bonding electrons moving onto Cl to form $\text{Cl}^-$. Unequal splitting of a bond where one atom keeps both electrons is heterolytic fission, so statement 3 is correct.

Since 1, 2 and 3 are all correct, the answer is the 1, 2, 3 combination.

options.A: Correct. All three statements are true. Cl is substituted by OH, OH- donates a lone pair as a nucleophile, and the C-Cl bond breaks heterolytically to give Cl-.
options.B: Incorrect. This option omits statement 3. The mechanism clearly shows heterolytic fission because the C-Cl bonding pair goes entirely to Cl- to form an ion, not one electron each.
options.C: Incorrect. This option omits statement 1. Students sometimes miss this because they focus on the arrows, but replacing Cl with OH is the classic definition of a (nucleophilic) substitution.
options.D: Incorrect. This option omits one or more true statements. A common trap is thinking OH- is only a base, but here it attacks carbon with its lone pair, so it is definitely a nucleophile.
